A horizon: The mineral soil layer nearest the surface, where organic matter mixes with sand, silt and clay. Humus often makes it darker, but color alone does not show how fertile or deep it is.
Abrasion: The wearing away of rock by sediment carried against it by water, wind or ice. Evidence includes scratches, polished surfaces and potholes. Unlike attrition, abrasion wears the surface being struck, not the transported particles themselves.
Absorption: The taking in of radiation by a material, which gains energy and usually warms. Dark ground often absorbs more sunlight than bright snow. Absorption differs from reflection, which sends radiation away, and transmission, which lets it pass through.
Abstraction: The removal of water by people from a river, lake or aquifer for uses such as irrigation or drinking water. A store shrinks when abstraction and other losses exceed recharge.
Active layer: The ground above permafrost that thaws in summer and freezes again in winter. Its thickness changes with local climate, vegetation and soil. Seasonal thaw of this layer does not necessarily mean that the underlying permafrost has disappeared.
Adiabatic cooling: Cooling as an air parcel expands when pressure falls, without exchanging heat with its surroundings. Rising air commonly cools this way.
Af: Köppen tropical rainforest climate: every month averages at least 18 °C and receives at least 60 mm of precipitation.
Age-progressive chain: A line of volcanoes that get older with distance from an active hotspot, recording the movement of the plate over it.
Air mass: A large body of air with broadly similar temperature and moisture characteristics acquired over a source region.
Albedo: The fraction of incoming sunlight reflected by a surface, expressed from zero to one or as a percentage. Fresh snow usually has a high albedo and dark soil a lower one. Albedo has no units; the reflected energy itself, in watts per square meter, is a flux.
Anticline: A fold with the oldest rocks in its core. In a simple upright anticline, the layers arch upwards and dip away from the center; overturned folds can have different geometry.
Anticyclone: An atmospheric circulation around a region of high pressure, commonly associated with sinking air. Surface winds turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Clear skies are common, but fog and low cloud can persist.
Appalachians: An ancient mountain belt in eastern North America, assembled through several Paleozoic collisions during the closing of oceans and formation of Pangaea.
Aquifer: A body of permeable rock or sediment that stores groundwater and lets useful amounts flow through it. The water fills connected pores or cracks; an aquifer is not usually an underground lake.
Aquitard: A layer of rock or sediment with low permeability that slows groundwater flow. It may confine an aquifer without being completely impermeable.
Arête: A narrow, sharp ridge formed where glaciers erode adjoining valleys or cirques. Striding Edge in the Lake District is an example.
Asthenosphere: A mechanically weak part of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere. It is predominantly solid rock that deforms slowly over geological time.
Astronomical unit: A defined length of 149,597,870,700 m, approximately Earth's mean distance from the Sun; abbreviated au or AU.
Attrition: The breakdown and rounding of transported particles as they collide with one another. Pebbles may become smaller and smoother during repeated transport. This differs from abrasion, in which those particles wear away the bed, bank or another fixed surface.
Axial tilt: The angle between a body's rotation axis and the perpendicular to its orbital plane. Earth's tilt is about 23.44°, and its axis keeps nearly the same direction over one orbit.
B horizon: A subsurface soil layer modified by soil-forming processes, often with an accumulation of clay or iron compounds moved from above. Compare its color and structure with the A horizon; a B horizon is not simply any material beneath topsoil.
Backslope: The main, usually steep section of a hillslope between its shoulder and footslope; material commonly moves through it downslope.
Barchan: A crescent-shaped dune formed where sand supply is limited and wind mainly blows from one direction. Its horns extend downwind.
Barrier: In a rain-shadow model, high ground that forces approaching air to rise; its height and orientation influence uplift.
Barrier island: An elongated sandy island lying roughly parallel to the coast, separated from the mainland by a lagoon or other shallow water.
Basalt: A fine-grained volcanic rock rich in iron- and magnesium-bearing minerals. Basaltic magma is generally less viscous than silica-rich magma.
Baseflow: The sustained part of river discharge supplied mainly by groundwater and other delayed stores between rainfall events.
Basin: A low area surrounded by higher ground. A drainage basin is the land area that sends water to a particular river, lake or other outlet.
Beheaded stream: A stream whose former headwaters have been diverted into another drainage system by river capture.
Biological weathering: The breakdown or chemical alteration of rock caused by living things. Roots can widen cracks, while organic acids from plants and microbes react with minerals. It works through mechanical and chemical processes rather than as a separate mechanism.
Biome: A large ecological region characterized by its vegetation and associated organisms, influenced strongly by climate, soils and disturbance.
Blockfield: An extensive cover of angular rock blocks, often found on cold upland plateaus. Frost action can contribute to its development, but the blocks may record a long history of weathering. Their presence alone does not prove that permafrost exists today.
Buys Ballot’s law: With your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, lower pressure generally lies to your left; the relation reverses in the Southern Hemisphere. Surface friction modifies the angle.
BWh: Köppen hot desert climate: precipitation falls below the desert aridity threshold and mean annual temperature is at least 18 °C.
Caldera: A large volcanic depression formed mainly when the ground collapses into an underlying magma reservoir after magma is withdrawn.
Caledonides: An ancient mountain belt formed during Paleozoic continental collisions, now exposed in places including Scotland, Scandinavia and Greenland.
Cambrian: The earliest period of the Paleozoic Era, beginning about 539 million years ago; its rocks record a major diversification of animal life.
Canary Current: The relatively cool eastern-boundary current flowing southward in the North Atlantic subtropical gyre. Coastal upwelling along northwest Africa can bring colder, nutrient-rich water to the surface.
Canyon: A deep valley with steep sides, commonly cut by a river into high ground such as a plateau. Rock resistance, uplift and changes in base level all affect how it develops.
Carbonation: Chemical weathering in which dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid that reacts with carbonate minerals such as calcite.
Catena: A sequence of soils down a slope whose differences are related to relief, drainage and the movement of sediment. A typical catena runs from freely drained soils on the crest to wetter soils on the footslope, although real sequences are rarely perfectly regular.
Cfb: Köppen temperate oceanic climate, with no dry season and warm rather than hot summers. London is a familiar example.
Chemical weathering: The alteration or dissolution of minerals through chemical reactions with water, gases and dissolved substances. Carbonation, hydrolysis and oxidation are examples. Unlike mechanical weathering, these reactions change mineral composition as well as the appearance of the rock.
Cirque: A bowl-shaped hollow with steep sides at the head of a glacial valley, enlarged by ice erosion and weathering. A lake, called a tarn, may occupy it after the ice retreats.
Clay: The finest soil mineral particles, less than 0.002 mm across in the USDA system. Their large surface area strongly affects water and nutrient retention.
Climate: The statistical pattern of weather over a long period, commonly 30 years, including averages, seasonal variation and extremes.
Clint: A block of limestone at the surface of a limestone pavement, separated from neighboring blocks by enlarged joints called grykes. Rainwater containing weak carbonic acid dissolves the rock along those joints and can also carve grooves into each clint.
Cold front: The advancing boundary of a colder air mass that displaces warmer air. Uplift near the front can produce cloud and rain, with weather depending on moisture and stability.
Colluvium: Loose sediment accumulated on or near the foot of a slope through gravity-driven movement and surface wash. It commonly contains a mixture of particle sizes. Unlike alluvium, it is not defined by deposition from a river channel.
Comma cloud: A curved, comma-like cloud pattern often seen in satellite views of developing or mature extratropical cyclones.
Competence: The size of the largest particle that a flow can transport under given conditions. Faster, more forceful flow can generally move coarser material. Competence differs from capacity, which concerns the total amount of sediment a flow can carry.
Compromise projection: A map projection that balances several kinds of distortion without preserving any one property exactly everywhere.
Conduit: A passage through which magma and volcanic gases rise toward an eruptive vent.
Cone of depression: A lowering of the water table or groundwater pressure surface around a pumping well. Water flows toward the well down this hydraulic gradient. The cone is a pattern in water levels, not an empty cone excavated in the rock.
Confined aquifer: A saturated permeable layer bounded above by a low-permeability layer. Water in a well rises to its pressure level, which may or may not reach the ground surface.
Confluence: The place where two streams or rivers meet. Below it, the river carries the water and sediment of both.
Conformal: Describing a map projection that preserves local angles and small shapes. This is useful for bearings, but area can become strongly distorted over a world map. A conformal projection cannot also preserve the area of every region.
Constructive wave: A classroom description of waves that tend to build a beach because swash carries more sediment landward than backwash removes. Whether a beach actually grows also depends on sediment supply, slope and changing conditions over the whole wave cycle.
Continental drift: The movement of continents over geological time, proposed by Alfred Wegener using evidence such as matching fossils and rock belts. Plate tectonics later supplied a wider explanation: continents move as parts of lithospheric plates that also include ocean floor.
Continental shelf: The gently sloping, submerged outer part of a continent, extending from the coast to the shelf break.
Continentality: The influence of distance from the ocean on a place’s climate. Inland locations often have larger seasonal temperature ranges because land heats and cools faster than water. Prevailing winds, elevation and nearby currents also affect the contrast.
Contour: A line on a map joining points at the same height above a stated datum. Close contours usually indicate steep ground and wider spacing a gentler slope. Contours are drawn on maps; they are not visible on the ground.
Contour interval: The vertical difference in height between neighboring contour lines. Check the map key before calculating a slope or hill height. On most maps the interval stays the same, while the spacing of the lines changes with the steepness of the ground.
Convergence: The movement of air toward an area, bringing neighboring flows together. Near the surface it can force air to rise, forming cloud and rain if enough moisture is present.
Convergent: Describing a plate boundary where plates move toward one another. Dense oceanic lithosphere may be subducted, while a continent–continent collision thickens the crust. The plate types determine whether a trench, volcanic arc or broad mountain belt develops.
Conveyor: A simplified description of interconnected deep and surface ocean circulation. Real flow involves branching currents, mixing, winds and density differences.
Coriolis: An apparent force caused by Earth’s rotation, which deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. Its effect on horizontal motion is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles.
Cover: Vegetation or plant residue that protects soil from direct raindrop impact and slows surface flow. Roots can also help hold particles together. The protective effect depends on the type, density and continuity of the cover.
Crest: The highest part of a hill or ridge. Soil thickness and drainage there depend on the local relief, geology and climate.
Crown: The upper edge of a landslide, where displaced material separates from stable ground. Cracks near the crown can outline the developing failure. It is distinct from the toe, where displaced material accumulates farther down the slope.
Crust: Earth's outermost compositional layer of solid rock. Oceanic crust averages about 7 km thick; continental crust commonly spans roughly 30–70 km.
Curie point: The temperature above which a material loses its spontaneous ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic ordering; about 580 °C for pure magnetite.
Cut bank: The eroding outer bank of a river bend, where the faster part of the flow commonly approaches the bank. A steep face or exposed roots can reveal active erosion. Deposition often occurs on a point bar across the channel.
Cyclone: A circulation around a low-pressure center: counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. Tropical and extratropical cyclones form through different processes.
Dam regulation: Changes to a river's discharge timing and magnitude caused by storing and releasing water from a reservoir.
Day length: The time between sunrise and sunset at a place. It varies mainly with latitude and the time of year because Earth has a tilted axis. Day length differs from the approximately 24-hour solar day, which includes darkness.
Declination: The angular position of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator, equivalent to the latitude of the subsolar point. It varies between about 23.44° north and south through the year and helps determine noon altitude and daylight duration.
Deep time: The immense timespan of geological history, extending back about 4.54 billion years to Earth's formation.
Deep water formation: The sinking of sufficiently dense surface seawater into deeper parts of the ocean. Cooling and increased salinity can contribute, especially at high latitudes. It is one part of a complex overturning circulation that also involves mixing and upwelling.
Deflation: The removal of loose surface particles by wind. Fine material may be carried away in suspension, leaving a coarser lag behind. Deflation removes sediment; abrasion is the wearing of surfaces by particles that the wind carries.
Delta: A body of sediment built where a river enters a sea or lake and deposits enough material to accumulate. Distributary channels often cross its surface.
Density: Mass divided by volume, measured in kg m⁻³. In most ocean conditions, cooling or increasing salinity makes seawater denser.
Depression: In meteorology, a region of low atmospheric pressure; in UK usage, commonly an extratropical cyclone.
Destructive wave: A teaching description for waves that tend to remove sediment from a beach, with strong backwash relative to swash. Net change also depends on sediment and wave conditions.
Discharge: The volume of water passing a river cross-section per unit time, usually measured in m³ s⁻¹. For mean velocity v and cross-sectional area A, Q = Av.
Distortion: A change in area, shape, distance or direction caused by projecting a curved surface onto a plane. No flat world map preserves all of them everywhere.
Divergence: The spreading of air away from an area. Surface divergence commonly accompanies sinking air in high-pressure systems, while divergence aloft can help sustain rising air below. Say whether you mean divergence near the surface or aloft.
Divergent: Describing a plate boundary where plates move apart. Mantle rock rises and can partly melt as pressure falls, producing new oceanic crust at ridges. Continental divergence may first form a rift before an ocean basin develops.
Doline: A closed depression in karst terrain, formed by dissolution or collapse of soluble rock. Also called a sinkhole; some drain underground and others hold water.
Drainage basin: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by the watershed.
Drawdown: A lowering of water level. In the tsunami lab it means the sea pulling back before some waves arrive; many tsunamis arrive without this warning. Groundwater drawdown means a lowered water table or pressure level.
Drumlin: An elongated hill streamlined beneath moving ice, commonly made of glacial sediment and sometimes containing bedrock. Its long axis usually follows former ice flow.
E horizon: A soil horizon depleted in materials such as clay, iron or organic compounds that have been carried away by percolating water. It often appears paler than adjacent layers. Not every soil profile contains a distinct E horizon.
Eastern boundary current: A current along the eastern side of an ocean basin, such as the Canary Current. In subtropical gyres these currents are usually broader, slower and cooler than western boundary currents, and coastal winds can also support upwelling.
Easting: A grid coordinate measuring distance east from a defined origin. Read eastings before northings in a grid reference.
Ecliptic: The plane of Earth’s orbit around the Sun, projected onto the sky as the Sun’s apparent annual path. The Moon’s orbital plane is inclined by about five degrees to it, so most new and full Moons do not produce eclipses.
El Niño: The warm phase of ENSO, marked by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific and coupled atmospheric changes.
Elbow of capture: A sharp bend marking where one drainage system has diverted water from another. It can help reconstruct river capture when combined with a wind gap or underfit valley. A sharp bend alone is not enough to prove capture.
Emission: The release of radiation by matter. Earth’s surface and atmosphere are cool enough that they emit mainly thermal infrared radiation. This differs from reflection, which redirects incoming radiation without first absorbing it.
Energy budget: An accounting of energy entering and leaving a system, such as Earth or a patch of ground. A persistent imbalance changes stored energy and can cause warming or cooling. A surface budget also includes evaporation and sensible heat transfers.
ENSO: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation is a coupled pattern of ocean and atmospheric variability in the tropical Pacific. Its warm and cool phases alter sea-surface temperature, trade winds and rainfall. These phases change the chances of certain weather rather than deciding every local event.
Epicenter: The point on Earth’s surface directly above the focus of an earthquake. It helps locate an event on a map, but the strongest shaking may occur elsewhere because of fault rupture, distance and local ground conditions.
Equal-area: Describing a projection that preserves the relative areas of regions on a map. Shapes and angles must be distorted to achieve this on a flat surface. Equal-area maps are useful when comparing the size or distribution of geographic regions.
Equator: The circle at zero degrees latitude, halfway between the poles. It divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is a parallel of latitude, whereas meridians of longitude run from pole to pole.
Equinox: The moment when the Sun is directly above the equator, in March and September. Day and night are then nearly equal everywhere, although daylight lasts slightly more than 12 hours because of how sunrise is defined and the bending of sunlight by the atmosphere.
Erg: A broad region covered by wind-deposited sand and dunes, often called a sand sea. An erg needs a supply of sand and conditions that allow it to accumulate. Many deserts instead have mainly rocky or gravel surfaces.
Erosion: The wearing away and removal of material by moving water, wind, ice or gravity. Weathering breaks down material in place.
Estuary: A partly enclosed coastal water body where freshwater meets and mixes with seawater, influenced by tides.
Eustatic: Describing a change in global mean sea level, for example from changing ocean-water volume or ocean-basin capacity.
Evaporative cooling: Cooling that occurs when evaporation uses energy from a surface and its surroundings. A moist surface can lose energy as latent heat instead of warming. The effect depends on available water, humidity, wind and incoming energy.
Evapotranspiration: The combined transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation and plant transpiration. It links soil moisture, vegetation and weather in a drainage-basin water balance. Potential evapotranspiration describes demand under adequate water supply, not necessarily the amount that actually occurs.
Extra-tropical: Outside the tropics. An extratropical cyclone is a storm system usually associated with fronts and horizontal temperature contrasts.
Eye: The relatively calm central region of a developed tropical cyclone, often with sinking air and reduced cloud. The surrounding eyewall contains much more vigorous convection and stronger winds. Passing into the eye does not mean that the storm has ended.
Eyewall: The ring of deep convection around a tropical cyclone’s eye, usually containing its strongest winds and heaviest rainfall. Its position and structure can change as the storm evolves. It differs from the calmer eye and the outer spiral rainbands.
Falling limb: The part of a hydrograph after its peak, when discharge decreases as stored water drains from a catchment. Its shape reflects delayed flow from soil, groundwater and channels. Rain may have stopped well before river discharge returns to its earlier level.
False origin: An offset origin used to keep map-grid coordinates convenient and usually positive. The British National Grid uses one southwest of Great Britain.
Fast cycle: Carbon exchanges among the atmosphere, living organisms, soils and upper ocean over relatively short timescales, from days to centuries.
Ferrel cell: The average circulation in the middle latitudes, with air moving poleward near the surface and equatorward aloft. Unlike the Hadley and polar cells, it is not driven directly by heating; passing weather systems largely maintain it.
Fissure eruption: An eruption in which magma emerges along an elongated crack rather than only from a single central vent. Lava fountains may form a line and then become concentrated at a few outlets. Basaltic fissure eruptions are common in Iceland and Hawaiʻi.
Floodplain: Relatively flat land beside a river that is shaped by channel migration and flood deposition and may be inundated when the river overflows.
Flux: A rate of transfer of a quantity such as water, carbon or energy; some uses express that rate per unit area.
Focus: The point within Earth where an earthquake rupture starts, also called the hypocenter. Rupture can then spread across a much larger fault surface. The epicenter is the point directly above it at the surface.
Föhn / chinook: A warm, often dry wind descending on the sheltered side of a mountain range. Air warms as it is compressed during descent, and moisture loss or differences in source air can intensify the effect. Föhn and chinook are regional names.
Foliation: A planar fabric in metamorphic rock, formed by aligned minerals or compositional bands. It commonly develops under directed stress. Foliation differs from sedimentary bedding, although both may appear as layers in an outcrop.
Footwall: The block of rock below an inclined fault plane. Identify it from the geometry of the plane before describing movement. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall; reverse motion is the opposite.
Fossil fuel: Coal, oil or natural gas formed from ancient organic material. Burning it transfers carbon from long-term geological stores to the atmosphere.
Four-figure grid reference: A reference identifying a 1 km square on a metric map grid, such as the US National Grid or the British National Grid, by its southwest corner. Read the easting first and then the northing. It identifies a square, not an exact point within it.
Fracture zone: A long scar on the seafloor that continues beyond the end of a transform fault offsetting a mid-ocean ridge. Unlike the transform fault, it is not an active plate boundary: both sides belong to the same plate.
Friction: Drag between moving air and the surface, which slows the wind and changes its direction. Near the ground this allows wind to cross isobars toward lower pressure. Higher in the atmosphere, surface friction is much weaker.
Frost shattering: Rock breakdown associated with freezing water and ice growth in cracks. Repeated freezing, thawing and ice segregation can widen the fractures.
Gas giant: A large planet made mainly of hydrogen and helium, such as Jupiter or Saturn. These planets have deep atmospheres above increasingly dense interiors and lack a solid surface like Earth’s. Their visible bands and storms occur within the atmosphere.
Geodynamo: The generation of Earth's magnetic field by motion of electrically conducting liquid metal in the outer core, influenced by Earth's rotation.
Geostrophic wind: An idealized wind in which the pressure-gradient force is balanced by Coriolis acceleration, so flow runs parallel to straight isobars. It is most useful above the frictional surface layer and away from the equator.
Glacial rebound: The gradual rise of land following the removal of a large ice load. The solid Earth adjusts as mantle material flows slowly over time. Rebound changes relative sea level locally, even while global mean sea level may rise.
Gley: Soil features associated with prolonged saturation and oxygen shortage, often including gray colors and rusty mottles from changes in iron chemistry.
Gnomon: The part of a sundial that casts a shadow. For a vertical gnomon on level ground, shadow length depends on its height and the Sun's altitude.
Gores: Tapered strips of a map designed to be fitted around a globe; small strips reduce the distortion needed to cover a sphere.
Gorge: A narrow, steep-sided valley. One way it can develop is through the retreat of a waterfall, leaving a deeply cut channel downstream. The surrounding rock and the river’s erosive history control its form.
Graticule: The network of meridians and parallels on a globe or map.
Greenhouse effect: Warming of a planet’s surface and lower atmosphere because gases and clouds absorb and emit thermal infrared radiation, slowing the loss of energy to space.
Grid square: An area identified by a map grid. In US National Grid and British National Grid notation, four, six and eight figures identify 1 km, 100 m and 10 m squares respectively.
Groyne: A structure extending across a beach to interrupt longshore sediment movement. Sand may build up on its up-drift side while the down-drift beach receives less. Its effects should be considered within the wider coastal sediment budget.
Gryke: A deepened joint or fissure separating clints on a limestone pavement. Weakly acidic water dissolves limestone along the fracture and widens it. Plants often occupy grykes because they trap soil and offer shelter.
Gulf Stream: A fast, warm western-boundary current in the North Atlantic, flowing from the Florida Straits along the eastern United States before turning offshore.
Gully: A channel cut into soil or unconsolidated material by concentrated runoff, larger and more persistent than a rill. In agricultural settings, a gully is generally too large to be removed by ordinary tillage and can expand through further erosion.
Guyot: A submerged seamount with a relatively flat summit, commonly formed when a volcanic island is eroded near sea level and later subsides.
Gyre: A large-scale rotating system of ocean currents. Winds, Earth’s rotation and the shapes of ocean basins help organize subtropical gyres. A gyre includes currents with different widths, speeds and temperatures rather than one uniform loop.
Hadley cell: The average tropical circulation in which air rises near the equatorial convergence zone, moves poleward aloft and descends in the subtropics. Near-surface return flow contributes to the trade winds. The real circulation shifts with seasons and continents.
Hanging valley: A tributary valley whose floor lies above the floor of the main glacial trough. The larger glacier commonly erodes more deeply than its tributary. After ice retreat, a waterfall may connect the two valley levels.
Hanging wall: The block above an inclined fault plane. In a normal fault it moves downward relative to the footwall, while in a reverse fault it moves upward. The names describe position relative to the plane, not present elevation.
Headward erosion: The extension of a valley or channel back toward its source by erosion. Over time it can shift a drainage divide and help one river capture another’s headwaters. It describes growth upstream, not water flowing uphill.
Helicoidal flow: A secondary, spiral-like circulation within a river bend, superimposed on the downstream current. Near-bed movement helps transfer sediment toward the inner bank, while strong flow near the outer bank promotes erosion. The pattern varies with channel shape and discharge.
Hill: An area of raised ground with relief above its surroundings, generally smaller than a mountain. Shape and local context matter: there is no universal height that separates the two. Contours can show its summit, slopes and relative height.
Horizon: A layer within a soil profile distinguished by properties such as color, texture, organic matter or mineral accumulation. Horizons develop through soil-forming processes. Their boundaries can be gradual, and a real profile need not contain every named horizon.
Horn: A sharp pyramidal mountain peak formed by erosion from glaciers on several sides; the Matterhorn is a well-known example.
Hotspot: A region of persistent volcanism that can occur within a plate or at a boundary. Many hotspots are associated with mantle upwelling; not all have an established deep plume origin.
Hydraulic action: Erosion caused by the force of moving water, including pressure fluctuations and water or trapped air acting within cracks. It can loosen material from a riverbank or coast. Abrasion adds the separate effect of sediment striking those surfaces.
Hydrograph: A graph showing how river discharge or water level changes with time. A storm hydrograph may be shown alongside a separate rainfall graph to compare timing and response.
Ice giant: Uranus or Neptune: a giant planet with a hydrogen–helium atmosphere and an interior rich in substances such as water, ammonia and methane. Despite the name, their interiors are not mostly solid ice.
Ice wedge: A wedge of ground ice formed as water enters thermal-contraction cracks and freezes repeatedly in permafrost.
Igneous: Describing rock formed when magma or lava cools and crystallizes. Slow cooling underground commonly produces larger crystals than rapid cooling at the surface. Texture therefore offers evidence of cooling history, although composition also affects the minerals present.
Incidence: The angle between incoming rays and a line perpendicular to the surface. A larger angle spreads the same beam over more ground. Solar altitude, by contrast, is measured up from the horizon.
Inner core: Earth’s solid central region, composed mainly of an iron-rich alloy and extending about 1,220 km from the center. High pressure keeps it solid despite its temperature. It is surrounded by the liquid outer core.
Insolation: Incoming solar radiation received at a surface. Its amount depends on the angle of the Sun, daylight duration and atmospheric conditions. Insolation is an energy input; air temperature also depends on energy losses, storage and transport.
Intensity: The strength of earthquake shaking and its effects at a particular place. It depends on the earthquake, distance, local ground and built structures.
Interception: The temporary capture of precipitation on leaves, branches and other surfaces before it reaches the ground. Some water evaporates and some drips or flows down stems. Interception changes the timing and amount of water entering soil.
Interfluve: Higher ground between neighboring river valleys or channels. Its slopes shed water toward the adjacent channels. An interfluve may lie within a larger drainage basin and is not necessarily the boundary of that entire basin.
International Date Line: The conventional boundary across which the civil calendar date changes, located broadly near 180 degrees longitude. Its course bends around countries and islands for practical reasons. It differs from the prime meridian, which defines zero longitude.
Intraplate volcanism: Volcanic activity occurring within a tectonic plate rather than along its boundary. Hawaiʻi is one example. Possible causes include mantle upwelling and lithospheric processes; its location alone does not establish the depth or structure of the magma source.
Inverse barometer: The tendency for sea level to rise where atmospheric pressure falls, and fall where pressure rises. A rough equilibrium estimate is about 1 cm per hectopascal. Storm surge also depends strongly on winds and coastal geometry.
Inversion: In structural geology, the uplift and shortening of a previously subsiding basin. A temperature inversion in meteorology is a different use of the word.
Isobar: A line joining places with the same atmospheric pressure on a weather chart. Closely spaced isobars indicate a large pressure gradient over a given distance. Wind also responds to Earth’s rotation and friction, so it does not simply follow that gradient.
Isostasy: The balance in which the lithosphere floats on the denser mantle beneath it. Adding or removing a large load, such as an ice sheet, makes the land slowly sink or rise. The mantle flows slowly as solid rock, not as a liquid.
ITCZ: The intertropical convergence zone: a shifting belt where tropical trade winds meet and moist air often rises. Its position varies with season, oceans and land heating.
K–Pg: The Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, about 66 million years ago, marking a major mass extinction associated with the Chicxulub impact and wider environmental change.
ka: A thousand years. Used with an age reference to express geological dates, for example 20 ka before present.
Kepler’s third law: For bodies orbiting the same dominant mass, orbital period squared is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis: T² ∝ a³.
Knoll: A small, usually rounded hill standing above nearby ground. On a contour map it commonly appears as nested closed lines with increasing elevation toward the center. Read the height labels to distinguish it from an enclosed depression.
Köppen: A climate classification system that groups places by long-term monthly temperature and precipitation. Its letter codes describe climatic thresholds and seasonality. Vegetation can suggest a climate, but one landscape or one day’s weather cannot determine the classification.
La Niña: The cool phase of ENSO, with unusually cool central and eastern equatorial Pacific surface waters and associated changes in tropical winds and rainfall.
Lag time: The time between peak rainfall and peak river discharge on a storm hydrograph. Some sources measure from the start or center of the rainfall instead, so check which is used.
Land breeze: A local wind from land toward the sea, commonly at night when land has cooled faster. Larger-scale winds can weaken or prevent it.
Lapse rate: The rate at which temperature changes with height in the atmosphere. An environmental lapse rate describes measured surrounding air; an adiabatic rate describes a rising or sinking parcel. An inversion occurs where temperature increases with height.
Latitude: The angular position of a place north or south of the equator, expressed in degrees. Latitude helps determine solar altitude and seasonal day length. Lines of equal latitude are parallels, unlike meridians, which measure longitude.
Leeward: The side sheltered from the prevailing wind. Descending air there often warms and has lower relative humidity.
Levée: Another spelling of levee: a raised bank beside a river, either built naturally by sediment deposited during floods or constructed to reduce flooding.
Levee: A raised bank beside a river, either built naturally by sediment deposited during floods or constructed to reduce flooding.
Light year: The distance light travels in a vacuum in one year (365.25 days): about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. It is a distance, not a length of time.
Limestone pavement: An exposed limestone surface divided into blocks called clints and solution-enlarged joints called grykes. Glacial stripping can expose the rock, after which chemical weathering enlarges fractures. The pavement records both exposure and later dissolution.
Lithification: The conversion of loose sediment into solid sedimentary rock, commonly through compaction and cementation. Pressure reduces pore space, while minerals can precipitate between grains. Lithification does not normally require the sediment to melt.
Lithosphere: Earth’s rigid outer mechanical layer, comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle. It is divided into tectonic plates and overlies the weaker asthenosphere. The lithosphere is therefore thicker than the crust alone.
Loam: A USDA soil-texture class containing a mixture of sand, silt and clay; loam is not defined as equal thirds of the three fractions.
Local stars: Stars in the Sun’s neighborhood, at distances usually given in light-years or parsecs. The nearest star system is Alpha Centauri.
Log spiral: A spiral whose distance from the center grows by the same factor with each turn. The coil in the Geologic time lab is not a log spiral: equal distance along it always means equal time.
Long profile: A plot of a river’s elevation against distance downstream. Many profiles become gentler toward the mouth, but resistant rock and uplift can interrupt a smooth curve. It differs from a cross-profile drawn across a valley.
Longitude: The angular position of a place east or west of the prime meridian, expressed up to 180 degrees. Earth turns through approximately 15 degrees per hour, linking longitude with local solar time. Civil time zones also reflect administrative choices.
Longshore drift: The net movement of beach sediment along a coast as oblique waves drive swash up the beach and gravity returns backwash downslope. Direction depends on wave approach. Structures that interrupt the supply can change beaches farther along the coast.
Longwave: Thermal infrared radiation emitted by Earth’s surface and atmosphere. It generally has longer wavelengths than most incoming solar radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and emit parts of this spectrum, influencing the rate at which energy escapes to space.
Lunar eclipse: An eclipse occurring when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow near full Moon and an orbital node. It can be penumbral, partial or total.
Ma: A million years. Often used for geological ages, such as 66 Ma; Myr commonly denotes a duration of a million years.
Magma: Partly or wholly molten rock beneath the surface, often containing crystals and dissolved gases. Molten rock erupted at the surface is called lava.
Magnetic reversal: A change in the polarity of Earth’s magnetic field. Magnetic minerals in cooling volcanic rock can preserve the field’s direction at the time they formed. Reversals occur at irregular intervals, so magnetic bands do not all represent equal durations.
Magnetic stripe: A band of oceanic crust whose magnetic minerals record a particular field polarity. Seafloor spreading carries newly formed crust away from a ridge, producing broadly matching polarity sequences on its two sides. Stripe widths also depend on spreading rate.
Magnitude: A measure of an earthquake’s overall size, commonly reported as moment magnitude based on fault area, slip and rock rigidity. An earthquake has one magnitude, but its shaking intensity varies from place to place. The scale is logarithmic.
Mantle: The rocky layer between Earth’s crust and core, extending to about 2,900 km depth. It is predominantly solid but can deform and circulate very slowly. Small amounts of partial melt occur in particular settings; it is not a global magma layer.
Mantle plume: An upwelling of unusually hot mantle material that may supply hotspot volcanism. It is mostly deforming solid rock, with partial melting possible near the top.
Mass movement: The downslope movement of rock or soil under gravity, including falls, slides and flows. Water can increase weight or pore pressure and may be mixed with the moving material. Gravity provides the driving force rather than a transporting river or wind.
Meander: A bend in a river channel. Outer-bank erosion and inner-bank deposition commonly move the bend across a floodplain; a cutoff can leave an oxbow lake.
Mechanical weathering: The physical breakdown of rock into smaller pieces without changing its mineral composition. Frost action and expansion or unloading can contribute. The fragments remain near their source until erosion transports them away.
Megathrust: A large, low-angle thrust fault at a subduction boundary. Sudden slip on its shallow offshore part can displace the seafloor and generate a tsunami.
Mercator: A conformal cylindrical map projection on which constant compass bearings plot as straight lines. It is useful for navigation, but areas are greatly enlarged toward the poles, so land areas on it cannot be compared directly.
Meridian: A line of longitude running from one pole to the other. A place’s local solar noon occurs when the Sun crosses its local meridian. Meridians meet at the poles, so the distance between adjacent longitudes decreases toward high latitudes.
Mesosphere: The atmospheric layer roughly 50–85 km above the surface, in which temperature generally falls with altitude. Many meteors become luminous here.
Metamorphic: Describing rock changed by heat, pressure or chemically active fluids while remaining mostly solid. New minerals or fabrics may develop. If the material melts and then crystallizes, the resulting rock is igneous instead.
Mid-ocean ridge: A submarine mountain system at a spreading boundary, where mantle upwelling and melting form new oceanic crust. Seafloor generally becomes older away from the spreading axis.
Midlatitude cyclone: An extratropical low-pressure system that develops from contrasts in temperature and is commonly associated with warm and cold fronts.
Misfit stream: A stream smaller than the valley it occupies, sometimes following river capture or the loss of former glacial meltwater discharge.
Mollisol: A USDA soil order characterized by a dark, base-rich surface horizon, often formed beneath grassland. It is not an exact synonym for every chernozem classification.
Moraine: An accumulation of debris transported or deposited by a glacier, including lateral, medial, terminal and ground moraines.
Mountain: A landform with substantial elevation and relief relative to its surroundings. There is no single globally accepted height separating mountains from hills.
Mouth: The place where a river enters a sea, lake or another river. Its form depends on sediment supply, water movement and local topography. Some mouths build deltas, while others form tidal estuaries or enter a larger channel directly.
Nabkha: A mound of windblown sediment accumulated around a shrub or other vegetation. The plant slows nearby airflow and traps moving grains. Its shape and growth reflect the interaction between vegetation, wind and sediment supply rather than wind direction alone.
NADW: North Atlantic Deep Water: a group of deep water masses formed through cooling, mixing and sinking in the North Atlantic and neighboring seas.
Neap tide: A period of relatively small tidal range, usually near the first and third quarters of the Moon. The Sun’s and Moon’s tide-generating effects partly oppose one another. Local coastal geometry and tidal timing modify the range observed.
Near side: The hemisphere of the Moon that always faces Earth, because the Moon rotates once per orbit. A slight wobble, called libration, lets us see a little more than half its surface over time.
Nick point: An abrupt steepening in a river’s long profile, also written knickpoint. A waterfall is one example. Resistant rock, uplift or a change in base level can produce one, and erosion may cause it to migrate upstream.
Nival: Describing a river regime strongly influenced by seasonal snowmelt. Discharge often increases during the thawing season. This differs from a glacial regime dominated by the melting of glacier ice.
Nivation: Weathering, meltwater movement and other processes around persistent snow patches that can help enlarge shallow hollows.
Node: One of the two places where the Moon’s orbital plane crosses Earth’s orbital plane. Eclipses require a new or full Moon close enough to a node for the Sun, Earth and Moon to align within the relevant shadow.
Noon altitude: The Sun’s angle above the horizon at local solar noon. In a simple geometric calculation it is 90° minus the absolute difference between latitude and solar declination. A negative value means the Sun remains below the horizon at noon.
Normal fault: A fault on which the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall. It commonly forms where the crust is being extended. Determine movement from displaced layers rather than the present height of the land surface alone.
Northing: A map-grid coordinate measuring distance north from the grid’s defined origin. Read it after the easting when giving a grid reference. The coordinate locates a position within a projected grid; it is not the same quantity as latitude.
O horizon: A soil layer dominated by organic material such as leaf litter and decomposing plant remains. It may overlie mineral horizons in some soils but be absent in others. Its thickness depends on inputs, decomposition and disturbance.
Occlusion: The process in which a cold front catches up with a warm front and lifts the intervening warm air away from the surface. The resulting occluded front can have extensive cloud and precipitation, depending on the air masses involved.
Oceanic crust: The outer rocky layer beneath most ocean basins, composed mainly of basalt and gabbro and averaging about seven kilometers thick. It forms at spreading ridges and is eventually recycled at subduction zones. It is only part of an oceanic plate.
Onshore flow: Air moving from the sea toward land. It can occur in a local sea breeze or within a larger weather system. The term describes direction relative to the coast, not a fixed compass bearing.
Orbital inclination: The angle between an orbital plane and a chosen reference plane. The Moon’s orbit is inclined by about five degrees to Earth’s orbital plane. This usually carries the Moon above or below the alignment required for an eclipse.
Orbital period: The time taken for a body to complete one orbit around another body. Planets farther from the Sun generally have longer periods: Mercury takes about 88 days and Neptune about 165 years. This differs from the body’s rotation period.
Order of magnitude: A scale step of a factor of ten. Quantities differing by three orders of magnitude differ by roughly a factor of one thousand.
Orogeny: A period or process of mountain building involving deformation and thickening of the crust. Plate collision and subduction are common settings. Mountains may later be eroded, leaving folded rocks and other evidence of an older mountain belt.
Orographic rainfall: Precipitation associated with air being lifted over high ground. Rising air expands and cools; if it becomes saturated, cloud can form and precipitation may follow. The lee side may receive less rain, depending on the wider weather pattern.
OSGB: Ordnance Survey Great Britain. OSGB36 is a geodetic datum used with the British National Grid; it differs from the global WGS84 reference system.
Outer core: Earth's liquid metallic layer, mainly iron with nickel and lighter elements, between about 2,890 and 5,150 km depth. It does not transmit shear waves.
Oxbow: A curved former meander channel separated from the main river. It may contain an oxbow lake or gradually fill with sediment.
Oxisol: A deeply weathered soil order common in humid tropical regions, typically rich in iron and aluminum oxides. Long weathering and leaching can leave a low supply of readily available nutrients. A red color alone is insufficient for classification.
Ozone layer: A region of the stratosphere with a relatively high concentration of ozone. Absorption of ultraviolet radiation helps warm this layer and reduces the amount reaching the ground. It is a diffuse region of gas, rather than a solid protective shell.
P-wave: A compressional seismic wave with particle motion parallel to its travel direction. It travels through solids and liquids and is the fastest seismic wave, so it arrives first.
Pangaea: A supercontinent assembled during the late Paleozoic and broken apart during the Mesozoic. Its reconstruction uses evidence from rocks, fossils, magnetism and continental margins. Pangaea was one of several supercontinents in Earth’s history, rather than Earth’s original crust.
Parallel: A line joining places at the same latitude. On a spherical globe, the equator is the largest parallel and the others become smaller toward the poles. Parallels do not intersect, unlike meridians of longitude, which meet at the poles.
Parsec: The distance at which one astronomical unit subtends one arcsecond; about 3.26 light-years, or 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m.
Partial melt: Melting of only part of a rock, because its constituent minerals do not all melt under the same conditions. Melt may separate and rise while solid material remains. This helps explain why magma differs in composition from its source rock.
Passive margin: A transition between continental and oceanic crust that is not an active plate boundary. Many Atlantic margins developed after continental rifting. Sediment accumulation, subsidence and occasional earthquakes can still occur, so passive does not mean completely inactive.
Patterned ground: Repeated ground patterns such as polygons, circles or stripes, produced by processes including frost sorting and thermal contraction in cold environments.
Peak discharge: The greatest rate of river flow during a specified event or period, measured in m³ s⁻¹.
Penumbra: The part of a shadow where the light source is only partly blocked. A Moon in Earth’s penumbra dims only slightly, far less than in the umbra.
Periglacial: Describing processes and landforms associated with cold ground, including freeze–thaw, frost sorting and thermal cracking. They may occur near glaciers or far from present ice. Relict features can remain after a region’s climate has become warmer.
Perihelion: The point in an orbit where a body is closest to the Sun. Earth reaches perihelion in early January. The changing distance affects incoming solar energy, while Earth’s axial tilt explains the opposite seasons of the two hemispheres.
Permafrost: Ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ice but need not be permanently ice-filled.
PGF: Pressure-gradient force: the force per unit mass associated with a pressure difference, directed from higher toward lower pressure.
Phase: The fraction and shape of the Moon’s sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth as viewing geometry changes through its orbit. Ordinary lunar phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow; that shadow is involved in a lunar eclipse.
Photosphere: The visible layer of the Sun from which most of its observed light escapes. Sunspots are relatively cooler, magnetically active regions within it.
Photosynthesis: The use of light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen-producing photosynthesis transfers carbon into living matter.
Pirate stream: The stream that gains water by capturing the headwaters of another drainage system. It may extend its valley by headward erosion. The term describes a changed drainage connection, not a different type of flowing water.
Plain: A broad area of relatively low relief, often but not always at low elevation. Plains can form by deposition, erosion or other processes. Flatness alone does not identify how a particular plain developed.
Planetary ring: A collection of particles orbiting a planet, ranging from fine dust to larger fragments. Saturn's rings consist mainly of water ice.
Plateau: An extensive area of elevated, relatively level ground. Rivers can dissect it into deep valleys and canyons while remnants of the high surface remain. A plateau describes broad relief rather than a particular rock type.
Plunge pool: A deep hollow at the foot of a waterfall, enlarged by turbulent water and sediment striking the bed. Undercutting and collapse may contribute to waterfall retreat. The pool’s form also depends on rock structure, discharge and sediment supply.
Pluvial: Describing a river regime mainly controlled by rainfall; its discharge seasonality reflects rainfall and catchment storage.
Polar cell: The average circulation in which cold air sinks near a pole and moves equatorward near the surface, returning poleward aloft. It forms part of a simplified global circulation model. Actual polar weather is less uniform than a single closed loop.
Pore pressure: The pressure of water or gas within pores in soil or rock. Increasing water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance to slope failure.
Pothole: A rounded hollow eroded into a rocky riverbed by turbulent water and circulating sediment. Trapped stones may assist abrasion as water swirls. It differs from a large plunge pool formed directly beneath a waterfall.
Power of ten: A number written as 10 raised to an exponent, used to express large or small quantities and compare their scales.
Precambrian: The informal span of Earth history before the Cambrian Period, covering the Hadean, Archean and Proterozoic eons.
Pressure difference: A difference in pressure between two places. It creates a pressure-gradient force that can start air moving.
Pressure gradient: The change in atmospheric pressure over a given distance. A larger gradient exerts a stronger pressure-gradient force on air. Closely spaced isobars often indicate a strong gradient, but wind also depends on friction and Earth’s rotation.
Prime meridian: The chosen zero of longitude. The modern reference meridian used by WGS84 lies about 102 m east of the historic Greenwich transit circle.
Projection: A mathematical method for representing positions on a curved surface on a flat map. Every world projection changes some combination of area, shape, distance or direction. Its suitability depends on which properties matter for the map’s intended use.
Pyroclastic: Describing fragmented volcanic material ejected during an explosive eruption, including ash, lapilli and larger blocks. Pyroclastic deposits differ from coherent lava flows. Particle size and deposit structure help reconstruct how material was transported.
Quadrature: The arrangement in which the Sun and Moon appear about 90 degrees apart from Earth, near a quarter Moon. This geometry is associated with neap tides, although local tides respond with delays and are shaped by their ocean basin.
R horizon: Hard bedrock beneath a soil profile. It differs from loose or partly weathered parent material usually labeled the C horizon. Roots and water may still penetrate joints even where the rock remains consolidated.
Radiosonde: An instrument package carried by a balloon that measures atmospheric properties such as temperature, humidity and pressure as it rises. Tracking its position also reveals winds. A sounding is a vertical sample at a time and place, not a complete atmospheric map.
Rain shadow: A relatively dry area on the sheltered side of high ground. Uplift and precipitation can remove moisture from approaching air, while descending air warms and its relative humidity falls. Prevailing winds influence the strength of the effect.
Rain splash: The detachment and movement of soil particles by raindrop impact. It can begin erosion before continuous runoff develops. Vegetation, litter and surface roughness reduce the direct impact on exposed mineral soil.
Rainband: An elongated or curved band of showers and thunderstorms within a storm system. Tropical cyclones commonly have spiral rainbands outside the eyewall. Their rainfall and winds can affect locations well beyond the eye, with large variation between storms.
Raised beach: A former beach now above present sea level because of land uplift, a fall in sea level, or both.
Ranker: A traditional soil term for a shallow, often acidic soil over hard, non-calcareous rock; commonly found on steep or exposed ground.
Recharge: The addition of water to an aquifer, usually as rainfall or surface water soaks downwards. Recharge can be slow and varies strongly with season and geology. Only part of the rain falling on the land above reaches the aquifer.
Regime: The characteristic seasonal pattern of river discharge, influenced by rainfall, snowmelt, storage and human regulation.
Relief: The variation in elevation within an area, often expressed as the difference between its highest and lowest points.
Residence time: The typical time material remains in a store. For a well-mixed store at steady state, mean residence time is its amount divided by its outflow rate.
Respiration: Processes that release energy from organic matter. Aerobic respiration consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water.
Resurgence: A place where water that flowed underground returns to the surface, often as a spring in karst terrain. Tracer studies can link a resurgence to a distant sinking stream. The visible outlet does not reveal the whole underground route.
Reverse fault: A fault on which the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall, commonly under compression. A low-angle reverse fault is called a thrust. Displaced rock layers help identify motion even after erosion changes the surface.
Revolution: The movement of one body around another along an orbit. Earth completes a revolution around the Sun in approximately one year. Rotation is the separate movement around its own axis, which produces the daily cycle of daylight and darkness.
Rhumb line: A path of constant compass bearing, shown as a straight line on a Mercator map. Except along a meridian or the equator, it is not the shortest route on a sphere.
Rift: An elongated region where the lithosphere is extending and thinning. Some continental rifts develop into ocean basins; others cease spreading.
Rill: A small channel cut into soil by concentrated surface runoff. Rills can often be removed by ordinary cultivation, unlike larger gullies. They show that water has begun collecting into preferred routes rather than flowing as a broad sheet.
Rising limb: The part of a hydrograph during which river discharge increases toward a peak. Its steepness reflects how quickly water reaches the channel. A rapid rise can follow intense rain or efficient runoff from saturated or paved surfaces.
Root: In isostasy, the thickened lower part of continental crust beneath a mountain belt. Less dense crust extends deeper into the mantle and helps support high topography. The term describes crustal structure, not a literal plant-like shape.
Rotation: The spinning of a body around its own axis. Earth’s rotation produces the day–night cycle and contributes to the apparent daily motion of the sky. It differs from revolution, which describes orbital motion around another body.
Rotational slump: A landslide in which a mass of soil or rock rotates along a curved slip surface. The upper part commonly drops and tilts back, while material moves outward near the toe. Water pressure can reduce the slope’s resistance to failure.
Run-up: The maximum elevation reached by a wave above a specified reference sea level as it moves onto land; distinct from inland inundation distance.
S-wave: A shear seismic wave with particle motion perpendicular to its travel direction. It propagates through solids but not through the liquid outer core.
Saffir–Simpson: A five-category hurricane scale based on maximum sustained wind speed. It does not rate rainfall, storm surge or the full impact of a cyclone.
Salinity: The concentration of dissolved salts in water. Evaporation and sea-ice formation can raise seawater salinity, while rainfall, river inflow and melting ice can lower it. Salinity and temperature together strongly influence seawater density.
Saltation: Transport in short hops or bounces, especially of sand grains moved by wind or flowing water.
Sand: Soil mineral particles 0.05–2 mm across in the USDA system. Other sediment classifications use a slightly different lower boundary.
Scale jump: A change between views representing very different sizes or distances. Each view needs its own scale because a single display cannot resolve all of them.
Sea breeze: A local wind blowing from sea toward land when daytime heating makes the land warmer than nearby water. A circulation develops with rising air over land and return flow aloft. Stronger background winds can weaken or overwhelm it.
Seafloor spreading: The formation and outward movement of oceanic crust at a spreading ridge. Magma cools to form new crust as the plates separate. Increasing rock ages and broadly matching magnetic polarity sequences on either side provide evidence for this process.
Seamount: An underwater mountain, usually volcanic. Seamounts need not lie on an age-progressive hotspot chain or have once stood above sea level.
Sediment budget: An accounting of sediment entering, leaving and being stored within a defined area. A beach can erode when losses exceed supply, even if deposition occurs briefly. State the boundaries and time period before comparing inputs and outputs.
Sedimentary: Describing rock formed from accumulated sediment or from chemical or biological precipitation. Clastic sediments commonly become rock through compaction and cementation. Bedding, grains and fossils can preserve evidence of the depositional environment.
Semi-diurnal tide: A tidal pattern with two high waters and two low waters in each lunar day, which averages about 24 hours 50 minutes.
Shear surface: A surface along which adjacent masses move relative to each other. In a landslide it separates moving material from the underlying slope and may be curved or nearly planar. It is distinct from the exposed cliff or landslide scar.
Shelf: The shallow, gently sloping submerged edge of a continent, extending toward a steeper continental slope. Shelf depth and shape influence tides, waves and storm surge. A shallow shelf can support greater wind-driven water-level rise for the same forcing.
Shelf fit: Comparison of continental margins, rather than modern coastlines, when reconstructing former continental positions. Sediment cover and deformation make the fit approximate.
Shield volcano: A broad volcano with gentle slopes built mainly by fluid lava flows, commonly basaltic. Mauna Loa is a classic example.
Shoaling: The change in a wave as it enters shallower water: it slows, its wavelength shortens, and its height may increase before breaking.
Shortwave: Radiation at the shorter wavelengths that carry most incoming solar energy, including visible light and parts of the ultraviolet and infrared spectrum. Earth’s much cooler surface emits mainly longwave radiation instead. Shortwave does not mean visible light alone.
Sidereal day: The time Earth takes to complete one rotation relative to distant stars, approximately 23 hours and 56 minutes. The mean solar day is longer because Earth also moves along its orbit and must turn farther to face the Sun again.
Silt: Soil mineral particles 0.002–0.05 mm across in the USDA system, intermediate between clay and sand.
Six-figure grid reference: A reference locating a 100 m square within a 1 km grid square. Read three easting figures before three northing figures. Adding figures improves reference precision, but the map and observation still limit accuracy.
Slip-off slope: The gently sloping inner bank of a river bend, where sediment tends to accumulate as a point bar. It contrasts with the steeper outer cut bank. Both develop as the bend migrates and its flow redistributes sediment.
Slow cycle: Carbon transfer through rocks, sediments and the deep Earth, involving weathering, burial, metamorphism and volcanism over geological timescales.
Snowmelt: Water released when accumulated snow changes from solid ice to liquid. Seasonal snowmelt can produce a strong spring or summer rise in river discharge. Its timing depends on temperature, radiation, elevation and snowpack depth.
Solar altitude: The angle of the Sun above the observer’s horizon. A higher Sun concentrates a beam over a smaller horizontal area and shortens a vertical object’s shadow. Altitude depends on latitude, date and time of day.
Solar constant: Total solar irradiance near Earth's mean orbital distance, about 1,361 W m⁻² on a surface perpendicular to the rays above the atmosphere. It varies slightly over time.
Solar day: The time between successive passages of the Sun across the local meridian, averaging 24 hours. It is slightly longer than a sidereal day because Earth also moves along its orbit while rotating.
Solar eclipse: An eclipse at new Moon, when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth close to an orbital node. With a close enough alignment, the Moon’s apparent size decides whether it is total or annular; a less exact alignment, or a view from outside the central shadow, gives a partial eclipse.
Solstice: The time when the Sun reaches its greatest northerly or southerly declination, in June and December. It brings the longest day of the year to one hemisphere and the shortest to the other.
Source: The starting point of a river’s channel, which may be a spring, a lake outlet or the convergence of small flows. The river also receives water along its course, so its source is not its only water input.
Spit: An elongated deposit of sand or shingle attached to land at one end and extending into water, commonly built by longshore sediment transport.
Spot height: The stated elevation of a particular point on a map, usually measured above a specified vertical datum. It provides a labeled value where contours show broader relief. It does not give the height of every nearby point.
Spreading rate: The speed at which plates separate at a spreading ridge, usually expressed in centimeters per year. A full spreading rate measures separation across both sides; a half rate measures one side’s motion relative to the ridge, so the convention matters.
Spring line: A line of springs where groundwater emerges along a geological or topographic boundary, often where permeable rock meets less permeable material. Its position reflects underground flow paths and can help explain the location of settlements.
Spring tide: A tide with a relatively large range, occurring around new and full Moon when solar and lunar tide-generating effects reinforce each other. Spring refers to the larger tidal range, rather than the season. Local coastlines and basins modify the response.
Spur: A ridge projecting from higher ground between valleys. Contours commonly form V or U shapes pointing downhill along it. In a stream valley, equivalent contour bends usually point uphill, helping distinguish the two on a map.
Squall line: A narrow, often violent band of convection, commonly along or ahead of a cold front.
Stack: An isolated pillar of coastal rock left by erosion and cliff retreat, sometimes after the collapse of a sea arch. Old Harry Rocks in Dorset are chalk stacks; nearby Durdle Door is a limestone arch.
Stage: The height of a river’s water surface above a specified gauge datum. Stage can be converted to discharge using a calibrated rating relationship, but they are different measurements. Changes in the channel can alter that relationship.
Stalactite: A mineral deposit hanging from a cave roof, commonly formed when dripping water loses carbon dioxide and deposits calcite. A stalagmite grows upward from the floor.
Still-water flood: Flooding measured by the water level with individual waves averaged out. Coastal still-water level includes the tide and any storm surge.
Store: A quantity of material or energy held within part of a system, such as water in a lake or carbon in vegetation. Inputs and outputs change the amount stored. A store is an amount; a flux is a transfer rate.
Storm surge: A rise in sea level above the expected tide, driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Coastal shape and water depth influence its size. Surge combines with tides and waves to determine coastal water levels and flooding.
Stratosphere: The atmospheric layer above the troposphere, extending to roughly 50 km altitude. Temperature generally increases with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. This stable layering limits vertical mixing, unlike the troposphere below.
Stratovolcano: A steep-sided volcano built up from alternating lava flows and fragmental deposits such as ash. Many form above subduction zones.
Strike-slip: Fault movement that is mainly horizontal and along the line of the fault. Some strike-slip faults form transform plate boundaries; others lie within plates.
Stump: The low remnant of an eroded sea stack, often visible only at low tide. Wave action and weathering reduce the isolated rock over time. The cave–arch–stack–stump sequence is useful, although real coasts can follow more complicated histories.
Subduction: The descent of one lithospheric plate beneath another into the mantle at a convergent boundary, commonly involving oceanic lithosphere.
Subtropical high: A region of relatively high atmospheric pressure commonly found near the poleward side of the Hadley circulation. Descending air tends to suppress cloud formation, helping explain many subtropical dry regions. Its position and strength vary with season and geography.
Sun path: The apparent arc followed by the Sun across the sky during a day. Its height, direction and duration above the horizon depend on latitude and date. Comparing paths explains seasonal changes in daylight and in the length of shadows.
Sunspot: A relatively cool, dark region of the solar photosphere associated with strong magnetic fields.
Supercontinent: A large assembly containing most of Earth’s continental landmasses. Earth’s history includes several cycles of assembly and break-up, of which Pangaea is the most recent.
Surface current: Flow in the upper ocean, driven by winds and pressure gradients and modified by rotation, coastlines and mixing.
Surface trace: In the fronts lab, the line where a sloping boundary between air masses meets Earth’s surface. It is plotted using weather observations. The edge of a visible cloud band may lie elsewhere and does not locate the front precisely.
Surface wave: A seismic wave that travels along Earth’s surface, including Love and Rayleigh waves. These waves can produce strong, prolonged ground motion, although damage also depends on frequency, distance, ground conditions and buildings. They differ from body waves traveling through Earth.
Suspension: Transport of fine sediment within moving water or air, kept aloft by turbulence rather than continuously resting on the bed or ground.
Swallow hole: An opening where a surface stream enters underground drainage, usually in karst. A doline or sinkhole is a depression and need not contain a sinking stream.
Syncline: A fold with the youngest rocks in its core. In a simple upright syncline, layers dip toward the center; erosion can leave either a ridge or valley above it.
Synodic month: The time from one lunar phase to the next occurrence of the same phase, averaging about 29.5 days. It is longer than the Moon’s orbital period relative to the stars because Earth also moves around the Sun.
Syzygy: An approximately straight-line alignment of three celestial bodies. In the Sun–Earth–Moon system it occurs around new and full Moon and contributes to spring tides. An eclipse also requires sufficiently close alignment with the relevant orbital node and shadow.
Teleconnection: A statistical relationship between climate or weather variations in distant regions, such as the influence of ENSO on rainfall probabilities.
Terminator: The line dividing the sunlit half of a planet or moon from its dark half. On Earth, places cross it at sunrise and sunset, and its angle to the poles changes with the seasons.
Terminator (day–night): The line dividing Earth’s sunlit half from its dark half. It moves as Earth turns, and its angle to the poles changes with the seasons.
Ternary plot: A triangular diagram showing three proportions whose sum is 100%. Each corner represents one pure component. In the soil-texture triangle, a sample’s sand, silt and clay percentages locate its texture class.
Terrane: A body of crust with a geological history distinct from neighboring regions, often joined to a continent by tectonic accretion.
Terrestrial planet: A planet with a predominantly rocky composition and a solid surface, such as Mercury, Venus, Earth or Mars. The category describes composition rather than habitability. These planets differ greatly in atmosphere, temperature and geological activity.
Texture: In soil science, the proportions of sand, silt and clay in the mineral fraction. Texture influences pore sizes, drainage and water retention. It differs from soil structure, which describes how particles are arranged into aggregates.
Thermal circulation: A circulation driven by differences in heating and the resulting pressure and density patterns. A sea breeze is a local example, with rising air over warmer land. Rotation and background winds alter larger-scale circulation.
Thermal equator: A belt of the highest mean temperatures at a given season. It shifts with seasonal heating and geography and does not always coincide with the geographic equator or ITCZ.
Thermohaline: Relating to seawater density differences caused by temperature and salinity. These contribute to ocean overturning alongside wind forcing and mixing.
Thermosphere: The very thin atmospheric layer above about 85 km, where temperature rises with altitude as gases absorb energetic solar radiation. Most auroras occur here.
Tidal bulge: An idealized elevation of the ocean surface in an equilibrium-tide model. Real tides are moving waves modified by basin shape, depth, rotation and coastlines.
Tidal range: The vertical difference between a high tide and the neighboring low tide at a location. It generally increases around spring tides and decreases around neap tides. Coastal shape, water depth and basin resonance strongly influence the local range.
Till: Unsorted sediment deposited directly by glacier ice, often containing a mixture from clay to boulders. Its poor sorting distinguishes it from many meltwater deposits reworked by flowing water. Till can form several types of glacial landform.
Time zone: A region using an agreed standard civil time. Boundaries follow political and practical choices and are not necessarily 15° wide.
Toe: The downslope end of a landslide or other mass-movement deposit. Displaced material may thicken or bulge there as it slows. It differs from the crown, where material separates from the stable slope.
Tombolo: A ridge of deposited sand or shingle connecting an island to the mainland or another island, often formed where wave refraction favors deposition.
Top of atmosphere: A reference level above most atmospheric absorption and scattering, used when describing incoming and outgoing radiation. Solar irradiance also needs a specified distance and surface orientation.
Trade winds: The prevailing tropical surface winds blowing toward the equatorial convergence zone. Earth’s rotation gives them an easterly component: they generally come from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere. Their position and strength vary seasonally.
Transfer: The movement of material or energy between stores within a system. In a drainage basin, infiltration transfers water from the surface into soil. A transfer describes a pathway or process; a flux quantifies its rate.
Transform: Describing a plate boundary where neighboring plates slide horizontally past one another. Crust is neither created nor destroyed along it. Earthquakes are common because friction locks the fault until built-up stress makes it slip.
Trench: A long, narrow depression in the seafloor associated with a subduction zone, where an oceanic plate bends down toward the mantle.
Tributary: A stream or river that joins a larger channel at a confluence. Its flow and sediment contribute to the downstream river. A tributary can have its own drainage basin nested within the larger river system.
Tropical cyclone: An organized, rotating low-pressure system with a warm core that develops over tropical or subtropical water. Strong storms can form an eye and eyewall. Hurricanes and typhoons are regional names for the same class of storm.
Tropics: The region between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, approximately 23.44 degrees north and south. The Sun can be directly overhead only within this belt, on dates determined by latitude. Tropical climates still vary greatly in rainfall and elevation.
Tropopause: The boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere, identified mainly by a change in the vertical temperature gradient. Its altitude varies with latitude and weather.
Troposphere: The lowest atmospheric layer, containing most of the air’s mass and nearly all weather. It is typically about 8 km deep near the poles and 16–18 km deep in the tropics.
True scale: A view in which all lengths are shown at the same scale, so sizes and distances can be compared directly. Any feature that is still enlarged or squeezed should be labeled.
Tsunami: A series of long waves generated by rapid displacement of water, most commonly during a large undersea earthquake. In shallow water they slow and can grow in height. Tsunamis are not caused by the normal daily tides.
U-trough: A valley with a broad floor and steep sides produced or enlarged by glacial erosion. It contrasts with the narrower V-shaped cross-section often associated with river incision. Later rivers and slope processes continue modifying the glacial valley.
Umbra: The central part of a shadow where the light source is completely obscured. During a total lunar eclipse the Moon lies within Earth’s umbra. The surrounding penumbra receives light from part of the source and produces a less complete darkening.
Upwelling: The movement of deeper water toward the surface, often driven by winds that move surface water away or by large-scale ocean circulation.
Urban heat island: An urban area that is warmer than nearby surroundings, often most evident at night. Surface materials, reduced evaporation, urban geometry and waste heat contribute.
